descriptions: the dependent's constant absence of the imagined (Triṃśikā 21)
the ultimate of dharmas, always thus, cognition-only-ness itself (Triṃśikā 25)
the non-existence of duality and the existence of that non-existence (Madhyāntavibhāga 1.14)
inconceivable, wholesome, constant, blissful — the liberation-body, the dharma-body (Triṃśikā 30)
undifferentiated in all beings; purified, it is tathāgatahood (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.37)
negations: neither existent nor non-existent, neither thus nor otherwise, neither born nor perishing (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 6.1)
neither other nor not other than the dependent (Triṃśikā 22)
relation_to_self: There is no self; the afflicted mind mistakes the store-consciousness for one. The ultimate is realized when the grasping of self and dharmas ceases and the basis is transformed.
relation_to_world: The world is the transformation of consciousness (cognition-only); the perfected nature is that world's true nature, reached when its imagined duality is seen through.
caveat: Yogācāra denies any self or creator; suchness is not a substance or a Brahman, and cognition-only is not a cosmic mind but the mind-streams of beings. The school rejects the Madhyamaka reading that even the dependent and the perfected are simply empty, and it teaches differing lineages rather than one destiny for all — reading it as 'one truth under many names' must keep these denials.

names.name: paramārtha-sat (the ultimately real: the causally efficacious particular)

descriptions: what is capable of causal efficacy is ultimately real (PV 3.3 conventional; NB 1.14–15)
cognition in itself is undivided; grasped and grasper are seen only by distorted vision (PV 3.354 conventional)
the mind is luminous by nature; the stains are adventitious (PV 2.208 conventional)
liberation comes from seeing emptiness (PV 2.253 conventional)
negations: no permanent means of knowledge, no creator God, no eternal self, no authorless Veda (PV Pramāṇasiddhi)
the particular is inexpressible; universals are not real
relation_to_self: There is no self; seeing a self is the root of attachment and all faults; seeing selflessness uproots it.
relation_to_world: The world of experience consists of momentary particulars; at the higher level it is cognition without real division into subject and object.
caveat: The pramāṇa school does not posit a single ultimate being: its 'ultimately real' is a plurality of momentary particulars, and at the cognition-only level non-dual cognition, not a universal consciousness; it explicitly refutes God and any permanent reality. The one-truth reading must record this denial.
